data.title: Frequency Exchange Announces Global Digital Premiere Of Superhuman 2: The Rebirth Series Featuring Nikki Wellness Technology And Closing Of Private Placement
data.description:
(TheNewswire)

Click Image To View Full Size

Vancouver, British Columbia, Canada – October 30, 2026 – TheNewswire - Frequency Exchange Corp. (“Frequency Exchange” or the “Company”) (OTCQB: FRECF) (FSE: YC6): is pleased to announce the worldwide digital premiere of Superhuman 2: The Rebirth, the new four-part

docuseries from award-winning filmmaker Caroline Cory, featuring NIKKI Wellness Technology, the

series’ principal partner and the Company’s flagship frequency-based wellness platform and wearable

device.

Following its Official Selection debut at the DaVinci International Film Festival on September 26, 2026,

and red-carpet global premiere in Beverly Hills on October 4, 2026, Superhuman 2: The Rebirth begins

its worldwide digital release today, October 30, 2026. The four-part series examines emerging

perspectives on human potential, perception and cognitive performance, bringing together a team of

leading subject matter experts to provide research-driven insights on innovative approaches to

wellness.

The worldwide online premiere began today at 12:00 P.M. PST, with live conversations and Q&A sessions featuring participants in the production. Stephen Davis, CEO of Frequency Exchange and founder of NIKKI Technology, participated in a live conversation and Q&A, followed by the premiere of the four-part docuseries. Tickets for the online event are available at watch.superhuman2.com, with each ticket providing access to the complete series for seven days.

“Today’s worldwide digital premiere represents an important visibility milestone for NIKKI and Frequency Exchange,” said Stephen Davis. “NIKKI’s prominent integration throughout Superhuman 2: The Rebirth, together with my participation in the live premiere, introduces the technology and our story to an international audience as we continue advancing our broader commercialization and market awareness strategies.”

The global digital release builds on the Company’s previously announced participation in Superhuman 2: The Rebirth and provides international exposure for NIKKI as Frequency Exchange continues to advance commercialization across North America, the Middle East and other international markets. Additional information regarding the premiere and Superhuman 2: The Rebirth is available at watch.superhuman2.com and wearenikki.com/superhuman.

Further to Frequency Exchange’s ongoing initiatives to advance commercialization and global expansion, the Company has closed the second and final tranche (the “Final Tranche”) of its previously announced Non-Brokered Private Placement (the “Private Placement”), further to its news releases dated July 31, 2026, and September 11, 2026.

The Company issued an additional 241,131 units (the “Units”) at $0.25 per Unit for proceeds of $60,282.75, bringing the total Private Placement to 1,949,361 Units for aggregate proceeds of $487,340.25 when combined with the first tranche closing. Each Unit consists of one common share and one-half of one common share purchase warrant (the “Warrant”).

Each Warrant is exercisable at $0.40 for a period of 12 months from the date of issuance. Warrants are subject to an acceleration clause whereby, if the volume-weighted average trading price of the Common Shares on the TSX Venture Exchange is at least $0.70 per Common Share for 10 consecutive trading days, the Company may, at its sole option, accelerate the expiry date of the Warrants to a date not less than twenty-one (21) days following notice of the accelerated expiry date by way of news release.

The Company issued 8,000 non-transferable finder’s warrants (the “Finder’s Warrants”) and paid a cash commission of $2,000 to Research Capital Corp. The Finder’s Warrants are exercisable at $0.40 per share for a period of 12 months from the date of issuance and are subject to the same acceleration clause as the Warrants. All securities issued in connection with the Final Tranche are subject to a statutory hold period expiring March 1, 2027.

Net proceeds are expected to be used to expand sales and marketing, increase inventory, advance technology and platform development, grow the Company's team, support international expansion, and for general working capital.

The Private Placement is subject to TSX Venture Exchange final approval.

About Superhuman 2: The Rebirth

Superhuman 2: The Rebirth is a four-part investigative docuseries by award-winning filmmaker Caroline Cory that examines emerging scientific perspectives on human potential, perception, and cognitive performance. As outlined on superhuman2.com, the series uses structured experiments and interviews to explore phenomena that challenge conventional models of cognition and sensory processing, providing viewers with a research-driven look at evolving wellness approaches in the field.

NIKKI Wellness Technology is prominently integrated throughout the docuseries as an emerging wellness technology. Its integration offers audiences additional context on frequency-based wellness programs within real-world observational settings, aligning with the background provided at wearenikki.com/superhuman.

About Frequency Exchange Corp.

Frequency Exchange Corp. (TSXV: FREQ | OTCQB: FRECF | FSE: YC6) is a technology company building the next generation of wearable digital wellness solutions through its flagship platform, NIKKI. Unlike traditional wearable devices that primarily monitor health metrics, NIKKI delivers personalized frequency-based wellness programs designed to support sleep, stress, recovery, energy and overall wellbeing. Originally developed through research supporting individuals living with Lyme disease, NIKKI has evolved into a scalable wearable digital wellness platform addressing some of today’s largest global health challenges.

For additional information, visit www.frequencyexchangecorp.com or www.wearenikki.com

data.title: Has the tech bubble burst? Why the Nasdaq's rough ride looks eerily like 2000.
data.description:
By Mark Hulbert

Friday's big plunge raises disturbing parallels with the top of the dot-com bubble

The parallels to the top of the dot-com bubble are close enough to be disturbing

Is that gushing sound from a bubble bursting?

It's an urgent question, given the stock market's rout on Friday, especially for the Nasdaq Composite Index COMP, which lost 748 points, or 2.9%. That certainly looks like bear-market behavior.

That's because big one-day plunges far more often than not occur during bear markets. Consider the 50 biggest one-day plunges for the Nasdaq since 1971, which is when the index was created. Forty-two of them - 84% - occurred during bear markets in the calendar maintained by Ned Davis Research. Since only 25% of all days since 1971 were in one of those bear markets, this means that big one-day plunges are associated with three-times-higher odds of occurring during a primary downtrend.

The parallels to the top of the dot-com bubble are close enough to be disturbing. Many investors labor under the illusion that the Nasdaq plunged almost immediately after hitting its all-time high on March 10, 2000 - in true bubble-bursting fashion. If that were so, then the market's recent behavior would look significantly different, since the Nasdaq today is only modestly below (5.1%) its all-time high from three weeks ago.

In fact, however, as you can see from the above chart, the Nasdaq didn't immediately plunge in March 2000. For the first three weeks following its high that month, this index was relatively flat - and only thereafter did the bottom drop out in a big way.

Will sentiment save the day?

One bright spot in the comparison of today with the top of the dot-com bubble is how quickly Nasdaq-oriented stock market-timers over the past few weeks have gone to cash. That's encouraging from a contrarian point of view, since market tops often are accompanied by stubbornly held bullishness.

Such stubbornness was very much in evidence at the top of the dot-com bubble. Consider the average recommended equity-market exposure among these Nasdaq-focused timers (as measured by the Hulbert Nasdaq Newsletter Sentiment Index, or HNNSI). This average actually increased over the three weeks subsequent to the Nasdaq's all-time high in 2000.

In contrast, the Nasdaq-focused market-timers today are far from stubborn. The HNNSI over the past three weeks has dropped 76 percentage points, and currently stands at 6.2% - indicating that these timers on average are now almost completely out of stocks.

The next several weeks therefore will be a test of contrarian analysis. Will its relatively upbeat analysis of current sentiment be strong enough to stop the stock market's strong downward momentum? Fasten your seatbelts.

Mark Hulbert is a regular contributor to MarketWatch. His Hulbert Ratings tracks investment newsletters that pay a flat fee to be audited. He can be reached at mark@hulbertratings.com

-Mark Hulbert

data.title: Starlink AI Acquisition in Deal to Take Spider Digital Technology Public
data.description:
By Stephen Nakrosis

Blank-check company Starlink AI Acquisition said it entered an agreement to take Spider Digital Technology, an operator of a cryptocurrency mining pool, public.

The deal assigns Spider Digital a valuation of $250 million for purposes of determining the merger consideration, the companies said.

Spider Digital has headquarters in Singapore, and is a technology company dedicated to blockchain research and ecosystem development, it said. The company has concentrated on cryptocurrency mining pool operations and operates its own proprietary mining pool system and maintains independent block generation capabilities, it added.

The deal is subject to approval from shareholders, New York Stock Exchange listing approval and other closing conditions.

data.title: Can Shopping Ever Be Fun Again? At Trunk Shows, the Answer Is Yes — WSJ
data.description:
By Chantal Fernandez | Photography by Amy Lombard for WSJ

On a recent Friday morning at a barn in Bedford, N.Y., I was on my hands and knees with two dozen other women as our fitness instructor, Carolynn Scull, reminded us we had more than endorphins to look forward to after 45 minutes of pulsing our limbs in the air.

"Guys, c'mon, you have champagne and beautiful, beautiful coats waiting for you!" said Scull, whose popular Pilates-inspired classes usually cost $55 a pop. That day, she was leading a complimentary workout at the Bedford Post Inn as a warm-up to a "shopping experience" — otherwise known as a trunk show — co-hosted by Max Mara, the Italian label known for camel-wool coats that can cost upward of $3,000.

After the class, I walked with sweaty would-be shoppers into a room with more than a dozen racks displaying capes, coats, jackets and knit dresses. A calligrapher was there to personalize free gifts with purchases, while two baristas manned an espresso bar set up for the occasion. Upstairs, Pilar DeMann, a makeup artist, was offering free eyebrow shaping services.

"I could walk into 10 stores and not buy anything," said Kerri Fitzpatrick, a 38-year-old shopper from Rye Brook, N.Y, after handing over her credit card to be swiped for a $1,860 furry black cape. "But when I'm at an event like this, I just feel like it's special."

Everything but the trunk

Decades ago, trunk shows involved designers like Bill Blass and Oscar de la Renta bringing actual trunks filled with embroidered gowns and luncheon-ready skirt suits to department stores and boutiques in major cities, where customers could place advance orders for the next season's clothes.

Now, as many department stores struggle to keep locations open, and as suburbs have grown wealthier, trunk shows are popping up in new places and taking new forms. No longer just events where designers use trunks full of samples to sell preorders, many combine the instant gratification of off-the-rack shopping with exclusive locations — private homes, hotels, yachts — and free perks.

The trunk shows at Laura Vinroot Poole's independent boutique Capitol, which has locations in Los Angeles and Charlotte, N.C., often feature live entertainment: Invited guests who shop can also watch Poole interview designers for her podcast. "They can come, have a juice or a tea, learn something, and then be more connected to a designer," she said.

Appearances by designers or brand insiders are still largely a component of modern trunk shows. Rubbing elbows with shoppers at the Bedford Post Inn were Max Mara USA's chief executive, Riccardo Broggi, and his wife.

The label hired City Country Beach, an agency that organizes private luxury experiences, to curate the guest list and set the program. "It's not just a bunch of racks and clothing," Jaimee Marano Lunderborg, City Country Beach co-founder, said of their events, which the agency doesn't call trunk shows.

Marano Lunderborg and Lizzi Bickford Meadow started the business in 2019 to advise brands on how to reach elite shoppers, especially those who had moved outside major cities. City Country Beach has since worked with labels including TWP, Balmain and Bulgari on events in places like Grosse Pointe, Mich. and Nantucket, Mass.

The agency now organizes about 50 events a year, according to its co-founders. Each relies on at least one well-connected local host, who invites their friends and family and is typically rewarded with a shopping credit.

Less scrolling, more shopping

Jennifer Galante Han, a digital strategy consultant, used the trunk-show model for La Volta, the consignment and vintage business she started earlier this year. At one of her first trunk shows, held in the private lounge of an upscale building in Manhattan's Tribeca neighborhood, Galante Han sold five-figures worth of luxury handbags and designer clothing in two hours, she said.

Her events have not had perks as lavish as others. But they have tapped into the social aspect of trunk shows, which has made them more compelling at a time when the internet has disrupted how we browse and socialize.

"Women want to shop together," Galante Han said, recalling the days when she would walk around malls with her friends growing up. Now, she added, "you're scrolling at midnight on your phone, and you're texting people, 'What do you think of this?' "

Zoe Gauntlett, whose business, Untold Luxury Group, uses trunk shows and personal shoppers to connect luxury brands with customers, said that group shopping can often inspire impulse buying.

For smaller or emerging labels, trunk shows are also opportunities to be discovered. Gauntlett specifically looks for brands that shoppers "wouldn't be able to walk into a department store and ordinarily see."

Independent designer Amir Taghi has had a front-row seat to the trunk-show revival. He started hosting them when he introduced his line of colorful, feminine womenswear in 2018. "It was kind of archaic," he said. "Now, all the brands are doing it, no matter what level they are."

Taghi generates most of his revenue through trunk shows: this year, sales at his events have totaled more than $1.5 million. On a busy month, he holds up to eight in six cities, attending most himself. His upscale clothes, priced between $800 and $3,600, are more popular in places like San Antonio and Aspen, Colo., than in New York.

Like others, Taghi typically taps local hosts for his trunk shows and thanks them with shopping credits. "There are some women, no matter how wealthy they are, that want a discount."
